title: Futur proche
description: Say what you are going to do with aller plus an infinitive.

guide.summary: The futur proche says what is going to happen: aller in the present plus a verb in the infinitive. It is the everyday way to talk about plans and things about to happen, where English says going to or will.

sections.title: How do you build it?
sections.text: Take aller in the present, matched to the subject, then the second verb in the infinitive. Only aller changes; the infinitive never does.
steps: Find the subject and take its row of aller.
Put the second verb in the infinitive: the dictionary form, with nothing changed.
Read the pair back: only the first verb may carry a subject ending.

examples.fr: Ce soir, nous allons regarder un film.
examples.en: Tonight we are going to watch a film.

watch: Never conjugate the second verb: nous allons dîner, not nous allons dînons.
Aller is irregular (va, vont, allons): do not build its forms from the infinitive.
Aller can be followed by aller itself: nous allons aller à Paris.

sections.title: Saying it is not going to happen
sections.text: Ne and pas close around the conjugated verb, which is aller. The infinitive stays behind them.
steps: Find the form of aller: that is the conjugated verb.
Put ne in front of it and pas straight after it.
Shorten ne to n’ before a vowel: n’allons, n’allez.
Leave the infinitive after pas, untouched.

examples.fr: Je ne vais pas me coucher tard.
examples.en: I am not going to go to bed late.
You are not going to wait long.

watch: The negation closes around aller, not around the infinitive: elles ne vont pas regarder.
Ne pas side by side belongs in front of an infinitive (ne pas fumer), not in front of a conjugated verb.
In speech people drop ne (je vais pas venir); written French keeps it.

sections.title: Three ways to ask
sections.text: Questions work on aller, exactly as in the present tense. The infinitive stays at the end.
steps: Write the statement first: subject + aller + infinitive.
Add est-ce que in front and change nothing else, or swap aller and the subject pronoun and join them with a hyphen.
With il, elle or on, inversion needs -t- between the two: va-t-il, va-t-elle.
Keep a space before the question mark.

examples.fr: Est-ce que vous allez prendre le train ?
examples.en: Are you going to take the train?

watch: Choose one way: never est-ce que together with inversion.
Inversion moves the pronoun behind the verb; it is not repeated in front (not il va-t-il).
Est-ce que is one block: que cannot be dropped.

sections.title: Words that point forward
sections.text: The futur proche usually comes with a time word. Anything built on hier or dernier / dernière looks back and cannot go with it.
steps: Read the verb: is it announcing something still to come?
Keep the words that look forward: demain, ce soir, bientôt, dans…, prochain(e).
Rule out hier and dernier / dernière: they belong to the past.

examples.fr: Nous allons voyager la semaine prochaine.
examples.en: We are going to travel next week.
It is going to snow tomorrow.

watch: Prochain(e) follows the noun: la semaine prochaine, not la prochaine semaine.
Ce soir is the evening ahead of you; hier soir was last night.

sections.title: Reflexive verbs: where does the pronoun go?
sections.text: The reflexive pronoun stands directly in front of the infinitive, and it changes with the subject. Se is only the dictionary form.
steps: Conjugate aller for the subject.
Swap the dictionary se for the pronoun of that same subject.
Place the pronoun immediately before the infinitive.
Elide me, te, se to m’, t’, s’ before a vowel or a silent h.

examples.en: I am going to get up early.
They are going to get dressed.

watch: The pronoun goes with the infinitive, not with aller: je vais me lever, not je me vais lever.
Moi and toi are stressed pronouns; they cannot stand in front of a verb here.
Without its pronoun the verb changes meaning: lever quelque chose is to lift something.

sections.title: Object pronouns before the infinitive
sections.text: A pronoun that replaces the object also sits just before the infinitive, because that is the verb it belongs to.
steps: Find the noun to replace, and check how the verb reaches it: directly, or through à?
Pick the pronoun, matching gender and number.
Put it directly before the infinitive, after the form of aller.
Elide le or la to l’ before a vowel or a silent h.

examples.en: I am going to do it tomorrow.
She is going to buy it.

watch: The pronoun never follows the verb: je vais les inviter, not je vais inviter les.
Les (them, as the thing acted on) is not leur (to them).
It goes before the infinitive, never before aller: elle va l’acheter, not elle l’va acheter.

sections.title: Present or futur proche?
sections.text: The simple present covers habits, general facts and what is happening right now. The futur proche covers plans and things about to happen, and it is what French normally uses where English says will.

rows: Ce soir, je vais manger dehors.

steps: Look for the clue: d’habitude, tous les jours and souvent point to the present.
Demain, ce soir, bientôt and la semaine prochaine point to the futur proche.
To move a present sentence into the futur proche, conjugate aller for the same subject and give the verb back its infinitive.

examples.fr: D’habitude je prends le bus, mais demain je vais prendre le train.
examples.en: I usually take the bus, but tomorrow I am going to take the train.
She is going to finish her work.

watch: Changing the tense means changing only aller: the main verb goes back to its infinitive.
French also has a simple future (je partirai), but for plans and near events the futur proche is the everyday choice.

Leave the second verb in the infinitive, whatever the subject is.

Leave the infinitive after pas, unchanged.

Choose one way to ask: intonation, est-ce que in front, or inversion with a hyphen.
With il, elle or on, inversion needs -t- between the verb and the pronoun.
Check that the form of aller still matches the subject.
Decide whether the verb points forward or back.
Keep the time words that look forward; rule out hier and dernier / dernière.
Remember that prochain(e) comes after the noun.
Conjugate aller for the subject.
Swap the dictionary se for the pronoun of that same subject.
Put that pronoun immediately before the infinitive, elided before a vowel or silent h.
Work out what the pronoun replaces and whether the verb reaches it directly or through à.
Pick the pronoun, checking gender and number.
Place it right before the infinitive, never before aller.
Read the time clue: a habit and now, or a plan and soon?
For a habit or a fact, conjugate the verb itself in the present.
For a plan, conjugate aller and give the main verb back its infinitive.

mistakes.why: That puts the pronoun in front of aller. It goes with the verb it is the object of, which is the infinitive.
Leur means to them, for people you speak or give something to. Faire les devoirs reaches its object directly, and devoirs are things.

exercises.instruction: Replace la lettre with a pronoun.
exercises.hint: The pronoun goes before the infinitive. Écrire starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: The pronoun does not go before vais, and la elides before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Je vais l’écrire: la becomes l’ before écrire and goes before the infinitive.

mistakes.why: The position is right, but the pronoun keeps its vowel in front of écrire, which starts with one. It has to elide.
The pronoun has been placed before aller. It belongs to écrire, so it stands directly in front of that verb.
A French object pronoun never follows the verb in a statement; it stands in front of the verb it belongs to.
Lettre is feminine, so a masculine pronoun does not fit, and it would elide before a vowel in any case.

exercises.hint: The pronoun belongs to acheter.
exercises.feedback: Put the pronoun before the infinitive, and elide it before the vowel.
exercises.explanation: Elle va l’acheter: the pronoun goes before acheter and becomes l’.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged, with the pronoun in front of aller. It belongs to acheter.
The position is now right, but the pronoun keeps its vowel in front of acheter, which begins with one.
The pronoun never comes after the verb in a statement; it goes in front of the verb it is the object of.

exercises.source: We are going to do it tomorrow.
exercises.hint: It becomes le. Where does it go?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun goes before the infinitive, not before aller.
exercises.explanation: Nous allons le faire: le goes directly before faire.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has been put in front of aller, where it does not belong: it goes with the infinitive.
An object pronoun stands before its verb, never after it.
Il is a subject pronoun. Standing in for the thing that receives the action needs an object pronoun.
Ferons is conjugated for nous. After aller the verb stays in the infinitive.

exercises.source: I am going to invite them on Saturday.
exercises.hint: Them is a direct object here. It goes before the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: One pronoun tile means to them. Inviter takes a direct object.
exercises.explanation: Je vais les inviter: les goes directly before inviter.

mistakes.why: Leur is for people you speak or give something to (je vais leur parler). Inviter reaches its object directly, with no à.
The pronoun has been put before aller. It is the object of inviter, so it stands right in front of that verb.
The pronoun never follows the verb here, and placed there it reads as inviting Saturday.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that replaces ta chambre.
exercises.hint: Chambre is feminine and a direct object.
exercises.feedback: The pronoun must be feminine singular.
exercises.explanation: Tu vas la ranger: la replaces ta chambre and goes before the infinitive.

mistakes.why: Le is masculine. Chambre is a feminine noun, and the pronoun copies the gender of the noun it replaces.
Les is plural. Ta chambre is one single room.
Lui means to him or to her, for a person. A room is a thing the verb reaches directly.
The pronoun only elides in front of a vowel or silent h; ranger begins with a consonant.

exercises.instruction: Put it in the futur proche.
exercises.hint: Use aller in the present, then the infinitive of the verb.
exercises.feedback: Mangeons must become an infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Nous allons manger: allons + manger.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged, in the simple present. The futur proche needs aller plus an infinitive.
The second verb still carries the nous ending. Only aller matches the subject.
Allez is the vous form of aller. The subject is nous.
That says we are going to the restaurant, a movement, and loses the verb of the sentence, which should follow aller in the infinitive.

exercises.instruction: Put it in the futur proche.
exercises.hint: Use aller for elle, then the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Finit must become an infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Elle va finir: va + finir.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged, in the simple present. The task is to move it into the futur proche.
Finit is conjugated for elle. After aller the second verb keeps its dictionary form.
Vas is the tu form of aller; the subject is elle.
Finira is the simple future of finir. Putting it after aller marks the future twice; the second verb stays in the infinitive.

exercises.instruction: Is it a habit or a plan? Choose the right form.
exercises.hint: D’habitude means usually.
exercises.feedback: A habit is not a plan for the future.
exercises.explanation: D’habitude, je prends le bus: habits use the simple present.

mistakes.why: That is the futur proche, which announces a plan. D’habitude marks something repeated, and French puts habits in the simple present.
That is the bare infinitive. With a subject in front, the verb has to be conjugated.

exercises.hint: Aller can be followed by its own infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Conjugate aller, then add the infinitive aller.
exercises.explanation: Nous allons aller: allons + the infinitive aller (we are going to go).

mistakes.why: That is only aller in the present (we are going). The futur proche needs a second verb, in the infinitive, after it.
Vont goes with ils or elles. The subject given is nous.
Allez is the vous form of aller. The subject given is nous.
The first verb has to match the subject; only the second one keeps its dictionary form.

exercises.instruction: Write se reposer in the futur proche.
exercises.source: Aujourd’hui, je travaille, mais demain je ____.
exercises.hint: Aller for je, then the reflexive pronoun for je, then the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Keep the pronoun before the infinitive and make it match je.
exercises.explanation: Demain je vais me reposer: vais + me + reposer, in contrast with the present je travaille.

mistakes.why: Reposer on its own means to rest something else. Resting yourself needs the reflexive pronoun before the infinitive.
Se is the dictionary form of the pronoun. It has to copy the subject, which is je.
The pronoun has slipped in front of aller. It belongs to the infinitive and stands just before it.
That is the simple present (I rest), which clashes with demain and with the contrast against je travaille.

exercises.source: Ce soir, tu vas regardes la télé ?
answers: Ce soir, tu vas regarder la télé ?
exercises.hint: Only aller changes with tu.
exercises.feedback: The second verb must be an infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Tu vas regarder: vas + the infinitive regarder.

answers: Ce soir, tu vas regardes la télé ?
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the second verb still carries the tu ending. Only aller matches the subject.

answers: Ce soir, tu regardes la télé ?
mistakes.why: That drops aller and gives a present-tense question. Keep the futur proche and fix the second verb instead.

answers: Ce soir, tu va regarder la télé ?
mistakes.why: The second verb is fixed, but the first one is now wrong: with tu, aller ends in -s.

answers: Ce soir, tu vas regardé la télé ?
mistakes.why: Regardé is the past participle, used with avoir. After aller the verb takes its dictionary form.
